questions.title: A levy on single-use containers
questions.stem:
Harbour City sends discarded takeaway containers to a landfill beside a fishing inlet. A local study values the extra external damage at 6 crowns per container throughout the relevant range. Firms and consumers pay none of this damage. Each week the competitive market follows Qd = 120 − 2Pc and Qs = 20 + 2Pp, where quantities are in thousands of containers and prices are crowns per container. Pc is the buyer's price; Pp is the seller's net receipt.

The council proposes a specific tax of 10 crowns. Assume full collection, linear curves and no change in other markets for parts (a)(i)–(vii). Fishing households benefit from less waste. A reuse deposit is another option, but collecting returned containers requires new facilities in outer districts. A small weekly survey found disposable packaging was most common among outlets without washing space.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the equilibrium price before intervention.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate equilibrium quantity and total external damage before intervention.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the buyer's and seller's prices after the proposed tax.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate the new weekly quantity and tax revenue. State the share of the per-unit levy borne by buyers.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Calculate the weekly external damage avoided under the proposed levy.

parts.label: a(vi)
parts.prompt: Using a diagram, explain why the proposed levy could reduce quantity below the socially efficient level.

parts.label: a(vii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the change in total weekly welfare from the proposed levy relative to no intervention. Treat tax revenue as a transfer.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the information and your knowledge of economics, recommend one policy for Harbour City to reduce the social cost of disposable containers.

steps.text: Set 120 − 2P = 20 + 2P (1). P = 25 crowns per container (1).
At P = 25, quantity = 70 thousand per week (1). Damage = 70,000 × 6 = 420,000 crowns per week (1). This is damage, not firms' production cost.
Pc = Pp + 10 (1). Solving 120 − 2(Pp + 10) = 20 + 2Pp gives Pp = 20 (1) and Pc = 30 crowns (1).
Quantity = 120 − 2 × 30 = 60 thousand (1). Revenue = 10 × 60,000 = 600,000 crowns per week (1). Buyers pay 5 more than before, or half the levy (1).
Avoided output = (70 − 60) thousand (1). Avoided damage = 10,000 × 6 = 60,000 crowns per week (1).

Draw demand, MPC and MSC, with MSC 6 crowns above MPC. Mark Q* where demand meets MSC. With Pc − Pp = 6, Q* = 64 thousand. The proposed 10-crown wedge produces 60 thousand. Units 60 to 64 thousand have benefit above full cost; preventing them sacrifices welfare. Up to two marks for a consistent diagram and two for explanation.

Lost private gains from trades no longer made form a triangle (1), ½ × 10 × 10,000 = 50,000 crowns (1). Avoided damage = 60,000 crowns (1). Net welfare improves by 10,000 crowns per week (1), despite overshooting the optimum. No second addition of revenue.

Introduce a levy nearer the estimated 6-crown marginal damage. It aligns the private decision with full marginal cost, reducing quantity from 70 to 64 thousand. Under the linear assumptions, the improvement relative to no intervention is ½ × 6 × 6,000 = 18,000 crowns weekly, greater than the 10,000 from the proposed rate. Revenue is a transfer but could finance washing facilities.

The damage estimate may omit marine harms or vary by location. A charge per container gives a weak incentive to redesign a container if all pay the same rate. Outlets without washing space have few substitutes and may pass costs to customers. A deposit can target litter more precisely when returns are convenient but collection requires resources. Pilot the levy and measure actual disposal and substitution; accept a justified deposit recommendation.

Best fit, 0–10. 0: no relevant response. 1–2: a policy is named with minimal reasoning. 3–4: a plausible policy with partial explanation. 5–6: a relevant mechanism and some use of the case, with limited trade-offs. 7–8: developed theory, relevant data and reasoned consideration of limitations. 9–10: a well-supported, feasible recommendation synthesising case evidence, economic reasoning and the most consequential trade-offs. Credit a different justified recommendation.

questions.title: An output gap and a repair programme
questions.stem:
Bracken's statistics office estimates current real GDP at 940 billion crowns and potential real GDP at 1,000 billion, at the same prices. An income survey estimates marginal propensities to save, pay net taxes and import at 0.20, 0.10 and 0.20 respectively, all measured per additional crown of national income. Use the simple open-economy multiplier with constant marginal leakages and no crowding out for the calculations.

A bridge repair plan would add 40 billion crowns to government purchases in the first year. A separate option is a temporary transfer to low-income households, some of which would be saved. Contractors in the construction sector report material shortages even though national unemployment is high. Public debt is 600 billion crowns, and the existing annual budget deficit is 18 billion. Monetary policy and prices may respond outside the simple model.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the recessionary output gap as a percentage of potential GDP.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Using the multiplier, calculate the predicted increase in equilibrium income and the resulting GDP if the full repair plan is an additional injection.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate the additional government purchases that would close the initial gap in this model and compare your result with the proposed plan.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: If GDP rises by 60 billion crowns, calculate the induced increase in net tax receipts and in imports under the stated propensities.

parts.label: a(vi)
parts.prompt: Assuming a 30 billion purchase, the 6 billion increase in net tax receipts and no other budget changes, calculate the new deficit and year-end debt. Explain the distinction.

parts.label: a(vii)
parts.prompt: Using an AD–AS diagram, explain why the repair plan might raise real GDP by less than its multiplier prediction.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the information and your knowledge of economics, recommend a fiscal response to the recessionary gap in Bracken.

steps.text: (1,000 − 940)/1,000 × 100 (1) = 6% below potential (1). Accept a signed gap of −6% if defined as actual minus potential.
Total marginal leakage = 0.20 + 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.50 (1). Multiplier = 1/0.50 = 2 (1).
Substitute 40 billion × 2 (1). Increase = 80 billion (1). Resulting GDP = 1,020 billion crowns at model prices (1). This is a demand-side projection.
Gap is 60 billion (1). Required injection = 60/2 = 30 billion (1). The plan exceeds that injection by 10 billion crowns (1); distinguish this from the 20 billion difference in predicted income.
Net taxes: 0.10 × 60 = 6 billion (1). Imports: 0.20 × 60 = 12 billion crowns (1).

New deficit = 18 + 30 − 6 = 42 billion crowns (1). If financed entirely by borrowing with no valuation changes or asset transactions, end debt = 600 + 42 = 642 billion (1). The deficit is an annual flow (1). Debt is the accumulated outstanding stock at a date (1).

Show AD shifting right and the economy moving toward capacity on a rising SRAS, with both a higher price level and higher real output (up to 2). Sectoral shortages, rising prices or tighter interest rates can limit the real expansion. A spending multiplier does not guarantee 1,020 billion of sustainable real output (up to 2).

Phase repairs, starting with projects using idle local labour. The model suggests an additional injection near 30 billion, while the full 40 billion would imply demand above potential. Repairs directly create orders and can raise future capacity. Prioritise projects with low import content and verifiable maintenance value rather than a fixed spending target.

The multiplier is uncertain and national slack does not remove local material bottlenecks. Automatic tax receipts partly offset the cost but projected debt still rises to 642 billion. A targeted transfer is quicker yet some of the initial payment is saved; compare its effective injection rather than applying the purchases multiplier to its face value. Stage commitments against unemployment, costs and repair bids. Credit a well-supported transfer or combined implementation of one principal policy.

Best fit, 0–10. 0: no relevant response. 1–2: a policy is named with minimal reasoning. 3–4: a plausible policy with partial explanation. 5–6: a relevant mechanism and some use of the case, with limited trade-offs. 7–8: developed theory, relevant data and reasoned consideration of limitations. 9–10: a well-supported, feasible recommendation synthesising case evidence, economic reasoning and the most consequential trade-offs. Credit a different justified recommendation.
